title: Circuit complexity lower bounds for quantum spin glasses
abstract: A central question in quantum information theory is the circuit complexity of states arising from standard many-body models. We study this question for quantum $p$-spin glasses, random Hamiltonians whose interactions act on $p$-tuples of qubits through Pauli strings. Anschuetz, Gamarnik, and Kiani (arXiv:2404.07231) showed that the optimum energy is separated from the best energy achievable by product states. This leaves open whether shallow circuits can close the gap, since even depth-one circuits can generate entanglement.   We show that the entanglement needed to close the product-state gap cannot be generated at shallow depth. When the average interaction degree grows with $n$, we prove that, for all sufficiently large fixed $p$, any circuit preparing an $n$-qubit state whose normalized energy is within a fixed positive constant of the optimum must have depth $Ω_p(\log n)$. In the bounded-average-degree regime, we prove a fixed-depth obstruction: for every fixed $D$, a sufficiently large degree prefactor rules out depth-$D$ preparation of near-ground states. Both results hold uniformly over circuits with an arbitrary number of ancilla qubits.   Our results give an obstruction in the spirit of the No Low-Energy Trivial States problem of Freedman and Hastings (arXiv:1301.1363), but for random quantum spin glasses rather than code-based Hamiltonians such as those of Anshu, Breuckmann, and Nirkhe (arXiv:2206.13228), whose ground states admit polynomial-size preparation circuits. This setting opens a probabilistic route to NLTS-like questions: we recast state-preparation lower bounds for random quantum Hamiltonians as uniform control of Gaussian processes indexed by shallow circuits.
summary: This paper establishes fundamental circuit complexity lower bounds for preparing near-ground states of random quantum $p$-spin glasses. By analyzing the required entanglement structure, the authors prove that achieving low energy necessitates deep quantum circuits unless the interaction structure is highly constrained. This offers a probabilistic route to understanding state preparation difficulty in disordered quantum matter.
main_problem: The central question is determining the circuit complexity (state preparation complexity) required to prepare quantum states near the ground state of random many-body Hamiltonians.
main_result: The authors prove that for quantum $p$-spin glasses, preparing near-ground states requires a minimum circuit depth of $\Omega(p \log n)$ in the growing average degree regime, and establishes a fixed-depth obstruction in the bounded average degree regime.
method: The analysis uses techniques involving studying the 'residual process' relative to product states and applying concentration inequalities (like Gaussian supremum bounds) to derive lower bounds on circuit depth.
model_or_system: The study focuses on quantum $p$-spin glasses, defined by random Hamiltonians acting on $n$ qubits via Pauli strings. The model is analyzed in different regimes: mean-field, growing average degree, and bounded average degree.
key_observables: Circuit depth ($D$), normalized energy of the prepared state relative to the true ground state optimum, and the residual term quantifying deviation from product states.
important_parameters: Number of qubits ($n$), spin interaction order ($p$), and parameters defining the sparsity/average degree ($\kappa_n$ or $\zeta$).
main_assumptions: The results hold uniformly over circuits with an arbitrary number of ancilla qubits, and comparisons are drawn to related models like code-based Hamiltonians.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the problem by contrasting ground state preparation complexity with product-state achievable energies. It then presents separate proofs for the growing average degree regime (yielding $\Omega(\log n)$ depth) and the bounded average degree regime (yielding fixed-depth obstructions). The context is set by comparing these findings to related problems like NLTS.
why_interesting: This work provides a rigorous, complexity-theoretic lower bound on how efficiently quantum information can be encoded in disordered physical systems, which has implications for understanding quantum simulation and computation limits.
